title: Applied Ethics: Dilemmas of Life, Technology, and Society

questions.question: Which set lists the four principles of bioethics identified by Beauchamp and Childress?
options: Liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
Utility, duty, virtue, care
Consent, privacy, profit, fairness
questions.rationale: Principlism works with four pillars — respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice — which collide in concrete cases.

questions.question: For consent to be genuinely informed, it must involve:
options: Understanding of the options and consequences, given voluntarily and free of coercion — not merely a signed form
A signature witnessed by two adults
Agreement with the doctor's recommendation
Payment for the procedure in advance
questions.rationale: Informed consent is the operational test of autonomy: comprehension plus voluntariness. A signed form without understanding fails the test.

questions.question: Why do many people approve diverting the trolley (killing one) but disapprove pushing the man off the footbridge (killing one)?
options: The numbers of deaths differ between the cases
Pushing is illegal while diverting is not
There is no morally relevant difference — the cases are identical
In the footbridge case the harm is used as a means, which the doctrine of double effect forbids
questions.rationale: Double effect distinguishes harm foreseen as a side effect of diverting the trolley from harm intended as the means of stopping it — the standard explanation of the asymmetry.

questions.question: Passive euthanasia is best defined as:
options: Administering a lethal injection at the patient's request
Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment and allowing the disease to take its course
Travelling abroad to obtain assisted dying
Increasing pain medication with no possibility of hastening death
questions.rationale: Passive euthanasia omits or withdraws treatment, letting the underlying condition cause death; active euthanasia directly administers death.

questions.question: The main trade-off of a 'sickest first' organ allocation rule is that it:
options: Ignores medical need entirely
Rewards patients who arrive early rather than the needy
May rescue the most dying patients while wasting organs on cases with little chance of benefit
Gives every patient an exactly equal chance
questions.rationale: Prioritising urgency can spend a scarce organ where benefit is low; utilitarian 'best prognosis' rules face the mirror-image objection of discriminating against the old and very sick.

questions.question: The primary source of AI bias in deployed systems is usually:
options: Patterns of historical injustice in the training data, reproduced and amplified by the model
Random hardware failures
Deliberate sabotage by programmers
Electricity costs during training
questions.rationale: Models learn statistical patterns from the past — biased hiring records or policing data — and present those patterns as objective mathematics.

questions.question: Why can't an AI system satisfy every fairness definition at once?
options: Computers are not fast enough to compute them all
The datasets are always too small
Fairness criteria such as group parity and equalised odds mathematically conflict when base rates differ between groups
Laws forbid measuring fairness directly
questions.rationale: Impossibility results (Kleinberg et al.) show the criteria cannot hold simultaneously except in degenerate cases — so which fairness to use is a political, contestable choice.

questions.question: The 'accountability gap' in AI ethics refers to the fact that:
options: AI systems cannot be audited at all
When an AI causes harm, responsibility diffuses — the developer points to the deployer, the deployer to the data
Only governments may be held responsible for software
Users must sign contracts to use AI systems
questions.rationale: Each actor in the chain can deflect blame ('the model decided'), which is why ethics demands accountability be built in by design — logs, audits, named owners.

questions.question: Ecocentrism, as in Aldo Leopold's land ethic, holds that moral value belongs to:
options: Humans only
All sentient beings individually
Every individual living organism
Whole ecological systems and species, not only their individual members
questions.rationale: Leopold enlarges the moral community to soils, waters, plants, and animals collectively — 'a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity of the biotic community'.

questions.question: According to the standard threshold defended by most ethicists, external whistle-blowing is justified when:
options: The harm is serious, internal channels are exhausted or complicit, and the evidence is documented
The employee finds any workplace practice annoying
The employee has already resigned for unrelated reasons
Never — loyalty to the employer is absolute
questions.rationale: The threshold balances loyalty against public protection: serious harm, failed internal channels, and documented evidence together convert silence into complicity.
